water supplies (including through recycled water
technologies), wastewater and stormwater treatment
systems, adequate electricity (including primarily
renewable energy), and transit and transportation
systems – comprises most of the projects challenged
in CEQA lawsuits and appeals. These include climate
resiliency systems such as enhanced flood protection
or wildfire prevention projects.
4
LOS ANGELES
6 7
Background
 In the current study, far more “infill” projects
in incorporated cities or areas surrounded by
previously developed unincorporated county land
were challenged; 64% of challenged projects are
infill, about 8% have no locational flexibility (e.g.,
mining projects), and only about 11% of projects are
located on previously undeveloped county lands.
Besides resort projects, greenfield projects are
located at the edge of existing urban communities
or are served by existing backbone infrastructure
such as freeways and water supply systems.
 In the current study, agencies prevailed against
opponents at an average rate of 75% – still
rewarding project opponents with judicial wins
more frequently than NEPA and other administrative
laws. The most detailed, time-consuming and costly
form of CEQA compliance, environmental impact
reports – which can take two to three years – were
found deficient in 23% of the decisions in the current
study. “Addenda” to EIRs, which serve as updates
to previous EIRs, were upheld in 81.5% of those
decisions. As in the 2015 study, EIRs were far more
likely to be challenged than any other form of CEQA
document – about 53% of appellate court decisions
were challenges to the sufficiency of EIRs (including
a few challenges to supplemental EIRs). This EIR
challenge pattern is consistent with our 2015 study
and our three trial court studies.
 The current study showed more projects that
qualified for “statutory exemptions” under CEQA
statutes adopted by the legislature and for
“categorical exemptions” under CEQA guidelines. As
the legislature has expanded the number of statutory
exemptions for housing and homeless shelters,
an uptick in appellate court decisions challenging
those exempt projects has followed. Although both
datasets showed the appellate courts are more
likely to uphold exemptions, exemption challenges
comprise 25% of appellate court decisions, more than
double the number of exemption appeal challenges
reported in the 2015 study.
The data from our current study follows. Appendix
A includes a brief overview of CEQA itself, and
Appendix B provides additional methodological
information about this updated study dataset.
The bottom line of the present study – like
our previous 2015 judicial outcome study and
our three trial court studies – is that CEQA
continues to be a formidable obstacle to
building anything in California, especially
anything near where anyone lives. The cost of
filing a CEQA lawsuit continues to be nominal,
and the act of filing even a meritless lawsuit
results in multiyear project delays, which
either increase project costs or derail projects
altogether. Anyone can file a CEQA lawsuit,
even anonymously, for any reason, including
to leverage money settlements or other economic
terms. No costs or other consequences are incurred
for filing meritless CEQA appeals, even for repeat
offenders who file more than a dozen serial lawsuits
against the same project. The adverse equity,
consumer, environmental and public health costs
of CEQA lawsuits are generally not acknowledged
in court pleadings, although in recent years pro-
housing advocates have begun to file amicus briefs
in some CEQA lawsuits. Median home prices were
$197,8007 in Los Angeles County when a project
was initially approved in 1999; decades of litigation
later, homes are still being built, but median home
prices have skyrocketed to well over $900,000.8
Taxpayer-funded transportation improvements
are first stalled, then rendered unfinanceable as
project costs and delays rise steeply – and drivers
spend ever longer times away from their families
commuting to distant homes they can afford.

affordable water and electricity are delayed for years
by CEQA studies spanning multiple years, only to be

Many stakeholders – the nonpartisan Little Hoover
Commission and Legislative Analyst’s Office
(responsible for overseeing state government
operations in California), Democratic and Republican
legislators, every governor holding office since 1990,
and hundreds of agencies and applicants seeking
to build anything anywhere – have recognized
CEQA as a massive obstacle or, as former Governor
Jerry Brown called it, a “blob.” CEQA’s status
quo defenders tout its necessity to “protect the
environment,” but thousands of environmental
protection laws and regulations are in effect today
that did not exist when CEQA was adopted in 1970 or
judicially expanded in 1972 to cover private projects
like building a home. The California Coastal Act, the
Endangered Species Act, the Clean Air and Clean
Water acts, the Occupational Safety and Health
Act, laws protecting public lands such as parks and
forests, and dozens of other major state and federal
environmental laws have cleaned up our air and water.
In 2016, the Obama Administration’s Environmental
Protection Agency announced that tailpipe emissions
of smog-forming pollutants had been reduced by
99%9 – without an electric vehicle mandate.
Today, CEQA’s staunchest defenders exploit CEQA
to block projects that comply with all existing
environmental protection laws and regulations. They
sue to get cash settlements to prevent new residents
from entering their neighborhoods or schools, to
oppose car-dependent development (despite the
fact that 97% of Californians drive daily10), to reject
market-rate housing in favor of exclusively taxpayer-
funded alternatives, to assert that unelected
community activists should control what can be
built anywhere, or to advance a vision of California
“de-growth” that prioritizes ideological climate
goals over actually reducing global greenhouse
gas emissions by making it affordable for people
and jobs to stay in California.11

Under AB 205, the CEC is the lead agency, under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), for environmental review and permitting for any facility that elects to opt into the CEC’s jurisdiction.
The Opt-In program requires the CEC to:
- Prepare an environmental impact report (EIR), mitigated negative declaration (MND), or negative declaration (ND), under CEQA.
- Certify compliance with requirements such as community benefits agreement and project labor agreements.
- Make a decision on whether to approve the project within 270 days of receiving a complete application.

Laura Klivans: Okay, and then I want to talk about data centers because that has really come into this conversation in the last few months, and we are already getting lots of comments on that. So, okay, talk about why people are concerned that data centers might be part of this proposition.
Ethan Elkind: Well, the issue is that they’re not explicitly excluded. This project — this proposition — does explicitly exclude high-speed rail, as I mentioned. It also excludes a Delta conveyance tunnel, but it did not exclude data centers, and the way that they’ve written what an essential project is for broadband infrastructure could arguably include data centers.
I don’t think it’s an open-and-shut case, but I think you’re gonna see developers of all types of projects try to argue that their projects are essential. And we don’t know how courts would decide on this. They’re supposed to be giving a lot of deference to industry under this proposition. And so I don’t think we have any assurance that data centers wouldn’t qualify for the benefits that Prop 45 would offer.
Laura Klivans: Interesting, because a lot of this debate about data centers is looking into the future and saying, well, maybe a lawsuit could happen. And from your position, Ethan Elkind, at UC Berkeley as a lawyer, it potentially could.
Ethan Elkind: Absolutely. That’s the whole issue with this. It’s going to create a lot of judicial uncertainty because there’s a lot of vagueness in how essential projects are defined. You’re going to want to see every single project developer argue that their project is essential.
Because of the way this proposition is written, we don’t know how courts are going to come out on this. So it does inject a lot of uncertainty. Like I said, they knew they could have excluded data centers. When they wrote this proposition, data centers were unpopular at the time. There’s a reason they excluded high-speed rail and Delta conveyance and some other things. They chose not to exclude data centers. So that, I think, is very telling on its face.
Laura Klivans: All right, well, briefly, when CEQA is at its best, what does it do?
Ethan Elkind: Well, I think it allows the public to have some information about what a project is going to do to the environment, to their community. It gives the public an opportunity to weigh in, and it gives decision-makers an opportunity to understand what they’re approving.
And more importantly than all of this is that when there are impacts, they’re required to be mitigated, again, when feasible. And so it not only gives the public and decision-makers information, it makes sure that we try to lessen the environmental impacts of big projects.
Laura Klivans: Thank you.

CEQA: Targeted Reforms for California’s Core Environmental Law
Report #279, May 2024
OVERVIEW
The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) remains an essential tool to protect the state’s environment, but can be improved through targeted, limited reforms, the Little Hoover Commission concluded in a recent report.
The new report, CEQA: Targeted Reforms for California’s Core Environmental Law (https://lhc.ca.gov/little-hoover-commission-offers-recommendations-for-ceqa-reform/), recommends six reforms to CEQA, including a raising of the standing requirement for filing a CEQA lawsuit, a restriction on late submission of public comment, and a broad exemption for infill housing. The Commission also recommended in-depth study of several issues related to CEQA.
CEQA was signed into law in 1970 with the goal of protecting and enhancing the environmental quality of California. It requires agencies to review projects to assess potential impacts to the environment, disclose those impacts to the public, and mitigate them to the extent possible. CEQA has been an important player in countless environmental victories, especially in disadvantaged communities that often bear the brunt of negative environmental impacts.
“CEQA is a successful landmark law that gives Californians a voice in how best to protect our great state,” said Commission Chair Pedro Nava. “With this report, the Commission seeks to identify small adjustments that could be made to help improve CEQA and ensure it is accomplishing what it was meant to.”
The Commission began a series of public hearings in March of 2023 to consider input from stakeholders, academic researchers, environmental experts, and policymakers regarding the current state of CEQA and whether changes to the law are necessary. The study culminated in a comprehensive report (https://lhc.ca.gov/little-hoover-commission-offers-recommendations-for-ceqa-reform/) in which the Commission offers suggestions for potential reforms to improve the functioning of CEQA.
The Commission’s recommendations include:
In order to lessen the use of CEQA for non-environmental goals, the Commission recommends strengthening the requirements needed to sue for alleged violations of the law. The state should adopt the standing requirement of the National Environmental Protection Act.
The Legislature should revise CEQA to limit the submission of public input that occurs after a public comment period.
The state should exempt all infill housing from CEQA review.
The state should provide funding for additional judicial training regarding CEQA.
The Legislature should reaffirm that courts should show greater deference to statute and CEQA guidelines.
The state should develop clearer parameters for significance thresholds and mitigations.
The report also recommended in-depth study of five additional topics related to CEQA:
The creation of specialized CEQA courts.
Translation of CEQA documents.
Bonding requirements for plaintiffs.
The effect of Vehicle Miles Traveled analysis.
Locking in analytical models for some reasonable period of time.
“Over time CEQA has been through piecemeal change,” said Janna Sidley, who chaired the Commission’s subcommittee on CEQA. “The Little Hoover Commission conducted an extensive study and is now providing six recommendations which improve the process while keeping a sharp eye on protecting California’s natural resources.”
“We hope this report helps reinforce CEQA’s original purpose while streamlining its processes,” said Dion Aroner, who also served on the CEQA subcommittee.
The Commission’s full report and recommendations can be found on the Little Hoover Commission website here (https://lhc.ca.gov/little-hoover-commission-offers-recommendations-for-ceqa-reform/).

Research Abstract:
This report details findings and analysis from the ongoing Comprehensive Assessment of Land Use Entitlements Study (CALES). CALES examines how jurisdictions approve housing development that would produce five or more units if built. CALES also analyzes how enforceable climate policies, such as the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), operate in relationship to the approval of new housing in urban and exurban areas and whether new housing development in both contexts faces opposition through lawsuits. All data points to local authority over land and local regulation as the most significant barrier to increasing the development of dense, infill housing and affordable housing in the study areas. Local governments could eliminate obstacles associated with state-level environmental regulation (and related litigation) by reforming their local law. Though community opposition to housing through litigation varies across cities, less than 3% of all approvals in our data faced litigation—with no meaningful difference between litigation rates for housing in urban or exurban contexts. Both urban multi-family and exurban subdivision development used similar expedited environmental review pathways intended to promote infill development; this is true for exurban development sited in high fire hazard areas.
Keywords: social equity, land use, housing, entitlement, CEQA, housing development, climate policies, local regulation, affordable housing, infill housing

CEQA: Study, Sue, Rinse, Repeat
2 3
Introduction
The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) was enacted unanimously
by a bipartisan legislature and signed by then-Governor Ronald Reagan in
1970. CEQA is a catchall statute requiring state and local agencies to consider
environmental impacts before approving or undertaking a construction
project, plan or regulation applicable to a construction project or the physical
environment. CEQA is older than the Endangered Species Act, Clean Air and
Clean Water acts, California Coastal Act, National Historic Preservation Act,
and thousands of other federal and state laws and regulations that ostensibly
protect the environment and public health. Any person or entity that
disagrees with an agency’s decision to approve or undertake a project that
is subject to CEQA can file a lawsuit in state court. CEQA trial and appellate
court proceedings typically take about five years to complete, and while
litigation is pending, most approved projects are stalled.
Jennifer Hernandez has practiced environmental and land use law in California
for 40 years; teaches environmental justice, land use and environmental law in
California law schools; serves on the boards of several nonprofit environmental
and other organizations; and has published several books and scores of articles
on CEQA, land use housing, climate and other topics. While the author is grateful
for the research assistance provided by the Independent Institute and other
Holland & Knight attorneys, the opinions and recommendations in this study are
the author’s and should not be attributed to any other person or organization, to
Holland & Knight or any client of the firm, or to the Independent Institute.
CEQA increasingly has been criticized as a major
reason California can’t build enough housing,
water, and transportation infrastructure or public
service facilities – including important projects
approved and funded by taxpayers – because all
projects subject to CEQA must also comply with
myriad other laws to protect human health and the
environment, only projects approved by elected and
appointed officials can be challenged, and litigation
delays increase project costs and sometimes derail
projects altogether. In 2024, California's preeminent
government oversight agency, the Little Hoover
Commission, issued a landmark report describing
CEQA's past successes and present challenges –
and recommended significant reforms.1 In 2025, the
California Assembly Select Committee on Permitting
Report likewise acknowledged challenges posed by
CEQA in achieving the state's housing, infrastructure
and climate goals.2 The need to reform CEQA and its
national equivalent, the National Environmental Policy
Act (NEPA), was even acknowledged by Democratic
Party candidates in the 2024 national election.
CEQA reform debates are highly politicized
because powerful stakeholders exploit CEQA
lawsuits and lawsuit threats to leverage economic
or environmental settlements and judicial outcomes
that cannot otherwise be realized by laws and
regulations. Often missing from political debates is
how CEQA is applied in practice – including which
projects are being sued and how those lawsuits are
resolved. For the past decade, we have been filling
that gap with actual CEQA litigation information.
This report includes 11 years of previously
unreported data about the judicial outcomes of
CEQA appeals. It concludes with analysis of how
California Proposition 45 on the November 2026
ballot offers voters the opportunity to accomplish
what decades of legislative efforts have not –
meaningful, structural CEQA reform.

Our 2015 report also described earlier CEQA judicial
outcome studies dating back to the first CEQA

Finally, this current report was informed by three
separate trial court studies. Those studies tabulated
all CEQA lawsuits filed in superior court statewide
over three separate three-year periods (trial court
studies).4 Evaluating appellate court outcomes in
the context of all CEQA lawsuits filed in trial court
allowed us to identify practices that were not evident
in the 2015 study.
The most noteworthy conclusions from the
comprehensive data evaluated in this study include:
 The current study found far more CEQA appeals
filed and decided than were reported in the 2015
study. As reported by the Little Hoover Commission5
and informed by our own three trial court studies (as
described below), about 200 CEQA lawsuits are filed
annually. In 2015, which evaluated only published
appellate court cases as described below, an average
of just 14.6 decisions were issued every year. In the
current study, an average of just under 21 decisions
were published and slightly more than 24 cases were
not published – totaling approximately 45 decisions
per year, more than twice the rate reported 2015
study.6 Appellate proceedings typically take about
three years to resolve, and projects do not qualify
for construction or grant funding while an appeal is
pending. Filing more CEQA appeals gives project
opponents and those seeking to leverage CEQA
lawsuits for economic or other nonenvironmental
reasons a “free” and low-cost litigation pathway for
further delay or seeking to derail approved projects.
Appeals prolong the 18-36 months typically required
to resolve trial court CEQA lawsuits.
 Housing remains the top target of CEQA appeals in
both the 2015 and updated studies, as well as in all
three trial court studies, as confirmed by the Little
Hoover Commission. Infrastructure needed to serve
new housing or development – such as augmenting
water supplies (including through recycled water
technologies), wastewater and stormwater treatment
systems, adequate electricity (including primarily
renewable energy), and transit and transportation
systems – comprises most of the projects challenged
in CEQA lawsuits and appeals. These include climate
resiliency systems such as enhanced flood protection
or wildfire prevention projects.
4
LOS ANGELES
6 7
Background
 In the current study, far more “infill” projects
in incorporated cities or areas surrounded by
previously developed unincorporated county land
were challenged; 64% of challenged projects are
infill, about 8% have no locational flexibility (e.g.,
mining projects), and only about 11% of projects are
located on previously undeveloped county lands.
Besides resort projects, greenfield projects are
located at the edge of existing urban communities
or are served by existing backbone infrastructure
such as freeways and water supply systems.
 In the current study, agencies prevailed against
opponents at an average rate of 75% – still
rewarding project opponents with judicial wins
more frequently than NEPA and other administrative
laws. The most detailed, time-consuming and costly
form of CEQA compliance, environmental impact
reports – which can take two to three years – were
found deficient in 23% of the decisions in the current
study. “Addenda” to EIRs, which serve as updates
to previous EIRs, were upheld in 81.5% of those
decisions. As in the 2015 study, EIRs were far more
likely to be challenged than any other form of CEQA
document – about 53% of appellate court decisions
were challenges to the sufficiency of EIRs (including
a few challenges to supplemental EIRs). This EIR
challenge pattern is consistent with our 2015 study
and our three trial court studies.
 The current study showed more projects that
qualified for “statutory exemptions” under CEQA
statutes adopted by the legislature and for
“categorical exemptions” under CEQA guidelines. As
the legislature has expanded the number of statutory
exemptions for housing and homeless shelters,
an uptick in appellate court decisions challenging
those exempt projects has followed. Although both
datasets showed the appellate courts are more
likely to uphold exemptions, exemption challenges
comprise 25% of appellate court decisions, more than
double the number of exemption appeal challenges
reported in the 2015 study.
The data from our current study follows. Appendix
A includes a brief overview of CEQA itself, and
Appendix B provides additional methodological
information about this updated study dataset.
The bottom line of the present study – like
our previous 2015 judicial outcome study and
our three trial court studies – is that CEQA
continues to be a formidable obstacle to
building anything in California, especially
anything near where anyone lives. The cost of
filing a CEQA lawsuit continues to be nominal,
and the act of filing even a meritless lawsuit
results in multiyear project delays, which
either increase project costs or derail projects
altogether. Anyone can file a CEQA lawsuit,
even anonymously, for any reason, including
to leverage money settlements or other economic
terms. No costs or other consequences are incurred
for filing meritless CEQA appeals, even for repeat
offenders who file more than a dozen serial lawsuits
against the same project. The adverse equity,
consumer, environmental and public health costs
of CEQA lawsuits are generally not acknowledged
in court pleadings, although in recent years pro-
housing advocates have begun to file amicus briefs
in some CEQA lawsuits. Median home prices were
$197,8007 in Los Angeles County when a project
was initially approved in 1999; decades of litigation
later, homes are still being built, but median home
prices have skyrocketed to well over $900,000.8
Taxpayer-funded transportation improvements
are first stalled, then rendered unfinanceable as
project costs and delays rise steeply – and drivers
spend ever longer times away from their families
commuting to distant homes they can afford.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Buried in the language of Proposition 45, the initiative that would overhaul California’s powerful law on environmental review, are provisions that would mean government agencies have to consult only with certain tribes in the state, and not others when they develop major projects.
Tribes that are federally recognized would be consulted; those without recognition would not.
This effort mirrors similar ones supported by tribes that have federal recognition to limit the say of tribes without it in recent years. Non-recognized tribes see it as another move by economically powerful tribes to protect their own interests and avoid having to negotiate with other local tribes over territorial disputes and how to best protect important sites.

“Our concern is that wealthy casino interests and political influence are being allowed to outweigh ancestral connections,” Andrew Salas, chairperson of the Gabrieleño Band of Mission Indians — Kizh Nation, said in a statement to The Times.
Proposition 45 on the Nov. 3 California ballot would create a streamlined environmental review process (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-45-ceqa-housing-data-center-voter-guide) for projects deemed “essential” — including most housing, transportation, water, health, wildfire mitigation, education, internet access and clean energy projects. The streamlining would mean stricter deadlines for review and court challenges, would bar local governments from requesting repeated analyses and allow developers to propose a single alternative with less environmental impact rather than several.
One of the largest contributors to the Yes on Prop 45 committee (https://yesonprop45.com/) is a federally recognized tribe, the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, which contributed $750,000.

The environmental review process under the California Environmental Quality Act, better known as CEQA, is one of the primary ways that tribes have a say over how the state and local governments develop land within their ancestral territories. It allows tribes to comment on how a proposed housing or infrastructure project might harm graves, ceremonial grounds or ancient villages. A separate law lets tribes comment on general plans that outline where developers can propose housing, and commercial and industrial facilities.
Tribal consultation differs from general public comment. It allows Indigenous leaders to discuss the location and details of sensitive information — such as burial sites — confidentially, before draft environmental reviews are published.

- Certify compliance with requirements such as community benefits agreement and project labor agreements.

Prop. 45: Will California Vote to Trade Environmental Regulation for Quicker Housing Development?
We’ll look at how changes could impact housing, data centers and more.
Oct 6, 2026
Updated Oct 7, 2026
Laura Klivans (https://www.kqed.org/author/lklivans) Ana De Almeida Amaral (https://www.kqed.org/author/aamaral)
Listen
In an aerial view, homes are seen under construction at a new housing development on July 1, 2025, in Richmond, California. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
Airdate: Wednesday, October 7, 2026 at 10 AM
The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), which requires most proposed public and private development projects to go through a thorough environmental impact review process, has long been blamed for slowing or stopping the development of new construction in the state. This November, Californians will vote on Proposition 45, which attempts to streamline CEQA review for certain “essential” projects. We’ll look at how changes could impact housing, data centers and more.
Guests:
Ethan Elkind, director of the Climate Program at the Center for Law, Energy and the Environment, UC Berkeley School of Law; podcast host, Climate Break
Jason Elliott, president, Versus Solutions; former deputy chief of staff to Governor Gavin Newsom, helped craft Prop 45
Jordan Grimes, legislative director, Greenbelt Alliance
Episode Transcript

Laura Klivans: Welcome to Forum . I’m Laura Klivans in for Mina Kim. When then-Governor Ronald Reagan signed the California Environmental Quality Act in 1970, it was meant to keep bulldozers from tearing up sensitive ecosystems. Fifty-six years later, CEQA is one of the most fiercely debated laws in the state. Its champions say it gives marginalized communities a means to stop harmful development. Critics say it’s been weaponized to block housing and drive up costs.
For decades, politicians wouldn’t go near CEQA reform, but as California’s housing crisis has deepened and clean energy projects must roll out at a faster pace, the calculation has shifted. Legislation passed last year made huge changes to the law, and this year, potentially more could come in the form of Proposition 45.
We’re going to hear from the people who’ve brought this initiative and those who oppose it, and we’ll talk about how unexpected players — data centers — have entered the conversation. But first, we’re joined by Ethan Elkind, Director of the Climate Program at UC Berkeley Center for Law, Energy, and the Environment. Welcome, Ethan.
Ethan Elkind: Thank you, Laura. Good to be with you.
Laura Klivans: Well, thanks for joining us, Ethan. I’ve spoken to you a lot. I’m a climate reporter here at KQED. Today we are talking about CEQA, which is, of course, the California Environmental Quality Act. Tell us, what is actually in this? What does it mean?
Ethan Elkind: Yes. Well, as you mentioned, it was signed by Ronald Reagan, and it was originally just proposed to apply to major public infrastructure projects. And if there are significant negative environmental impacts, then decision-makers would have to mitigate those impacts if it’s feasible to do so.
Now, if it is not feasible, the project is just going to have a lot of impacts and there’s nothing you can really do, then the project could proceed. But basically, it was a way to inform decision-makers and inform the public about the project’s scope of impacts, and also potential alternatives to the project.
Now, the courts have dramatically expanded it. And there was a big decision in 1972 that basically said now all projects that require some sort of public approval, which is basically all projects, now have to go through the CEQA process. So it has been greatly expanded by the courts based on what Ronald Reagan thought he was signing — I’m assuming what he thought he was signing in 1970.
Laura Klivans: So it started out as something that’s like, this is about, you know, dams. And then now it’s like, this is about your neighbor’s house.
Ethan Elkind: Yes, although many projects are exempt or face very streamlined review. Now, the biggest projects have to undergo what’s called an environmental impact report. And these can be like multiple phone-book-sized documents that look at all types of impacts. But that’s really just a very small percentage of projects.
And then once those environmental impact reports come out, and really almost all steps in the process of CEQA, there’s opportunities for the public to sue if they feel like decision-makers have done an inadequate job in analyzing those impacts. And that’s really where a lot of the controversy around CEQA has come into play, that it provides members of the public with opportunities to have pretty extreme leverage in some cases over particularly large projects.
Laura Klivans: And so talk me through that. CEQA has been criticized for stunting development. So take us through the process of what a developer actually must do to comply with it.
Ethan Elkind: Well, like I say, it really depends on how big the project is. Many projects are completely exempt. If a project just has a very narrow set of likely impacts, then often it’s very easy to just come up with some simple mitigation measures, and then the developer can move forward.
But for big projects that have a lot of impacts — think of, like, a big industrial project, maybe a large subdivision out on green space, farmland, maybe transmission lines, logging projects, et cetera. Those kinds of projects have multiple types of impacts. They’ll impact the air quality, they’ll impact endangered species habitat, they will impact noise, visual aesthetics, archaeological resources, historical resources. All of these types of impacts have to be analyzed for these large projects and mitigated where feasible.
And at that point, the public, if there’s maybe an economic competitor, if they’re neighbors, uh… There’s environmental groups — they have the ability to sue if those impacts are not analyzed properly and the mitigation measures aren’t adequate, uh… And so that’s really where the leverage comes into play, and it’s often at the very end of the process when a developer’s already sort of lined up a lot of their financing, figured out where legally they’re allowed to proceed under the land-use laws.
And so for developers, for industry, they hate this law because it injects a huge amount of uncertainty really right at the end of the process. And by delaying projects, that costs money. I mean, time is money for developers. And while the law is not meant to stop any projects, it can effectively do so if there’s litigation that draws out the timelines by many years.
Laura Klivans: Okay. And then, so how long does CEQA review actually take in some of those instances? On average, maybe, and then in the worst-case scenarios.
Ethan Elkind: Yeah, I haven’t really looked at the data on this. I mean, in some cases, there have been some high-profile cases that have lasted decades. Those are very controversial, very large projects. And usually, there’s other factors involved. But I would guess that’s probably a year or two to resolve.
Laura Klivans: And then CEQA — you know, we see CEQA come up again for folks who are just tuning in, the California Environmental Quality Act. Ethan Elkind: Well, this is the issue that there are these high-profile lawsuits that just look kind of ridiculous on their face, and then people throw up their hands and say CEQA is being abused and it really should go away.
So in this particular case, you had student housing proposed at People’s Park in Berkeley, and the courts ruled that essentially students were an environmental impact. I mean, I’m sort of saying this a little superficially here, but the result of it was to hold up a really badly needed student housing project that the university wanted to move forward on.
And the legislature immediately stepped in in response to the negative publicity, and they amended the law in an emergency statute so that it would go into effect right away instead of in the next year to overrule what the court had decided.
But in reality, there are less than 200 lawsuits a year. This has been very well tracked by multiple sources. So litigation is actually quite infrequent. But when it does happen, it makes a lot of headlines. And so you get a sort of anecdotally driven debate on CEQA. We’re not really looking at the actual numbers, which are quite rare.
Although I will say that the threat of lawsuits is very — has a really chilling effect. It’s a big deterrent for a lot of developers. A lot of developers I spoke to, if they think there’s any risk of a CEQA lawsuit for a project, they won’t move forward. They’ll choose a different area or they’ll design the project differently. Laura Klivans: Okay.

Ethan Elkind: Well, Prop 45 would dramatically scale back the scope and timeline of environmental review for what its backers have called essential projects. And these are high-impact, often very polluting types of projects.
So housing, which would mean all types of subdivisions, large-scale subdivisions over open space that generate a lot of traffic and can eat up a lot of endangered species habitat. Renewable energy projects. All types of transportation projects, with the exception of high-speed rail, so freeways, freeway widening. Uh… Dams and irrigation projects, logging projects. So it’s a wide swath of projects. These are backed by some of the big industry groups in the state. This proposition is backed by some big industry groups in the state. And it would essentially allow the developer to define the scope of the impact. So it would be a greatly narrowed set of impacts.
There would be a dramatically reduced shot clock on deeming the CEQA review complete, so just 90 days, with some exceptions. And it will be really hard for the public to be able to challenge any of these CEQA decisions. It raises the bar for any sort of judicial attacks on what decision-makers have done on CEQA. It’s hard and will make it hard for the legislature to amend this proposition. It would require a two-thirds majority of the legislature to amend itself.

It also excludes a Delta conveyance tunnel, but it did not exclude data centers, and the way that they’ve written what an essential project is for broadband infrastructure could arguably include data centers.
I don’t think it’s an open-and-shut case, but I think you’re gonna see developers of all types of projects try to argue that their projects are essential. And we don’t know how courts would decide on this. They’re supposed to be giving a lot of deference to industry under this proposition. Or email your comments and questions to [email protected] (https://www.kqed.org/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#d3b5bca1a6be93b8a2b6b7fdbca1b4). Find us on Discord, Bluesky, Facebook, and Instagram. All those places, we’re at KQED Forum. Or give us a call now at 866-733-6786.
This is Forum . I’m Laura Klivans in for Mina Kim. We’re talking about Proposition 45, a ballot measure proposing changes to California’s landmark environmental protection law, which is called CEQA. That just rolls off the tongue.
And we’re joined by Ethan Elkind. He’s the director of the Climate Program at UC Berkeley Center for Law, Energy, and the Environment. And we are now welcoming in two additional people.
We have Jason Elliott. He is the president of policy consulting firm Versus Solutions. He helped craft Prop 45. And we also have Jordan Grimes. He’s the legislative director with the environmental nonprofit Greenbelt Alliance. He’s part of the Know on Prop 45 campaign.
So you have heard Ethan. He shared his interpretations of CEQA and Prop 45. Jason, I saw that you were shaking your head a bit on some of that stuff. Give us what that shaking of a head was about.
Jason Elliott: First of all, thanks for hosting this Forum today. I think that everyone wants to talk for an hour about the intricacies of environmental review law.
Laura Klivans: So stick with us, folks. That and Taylor Swift.
Jason Elliott: I can get Taylor Swift in here somehow.
So I appreciate the professor’s blessings upon Ethan for explaining CEQA, which is one of the most complicated laws in California. I do take a little bit of exception to some of the characterization of Prop 45, because I’ve heard some of those talking points, and they’re the talking points of our opponents.
But let’s talk about what is happening here. Look, California has decided what it wants. It wants cleaner air. It wants clean water. It wants affordable and clean energy. It wants housing you can afford.
Frankly, over the years, voters have voted on and the legislature has passed a number of bills to move us towards those goals. We funded it, we’ve passed bonds, we’ve done spending programs, but what we haven’t done is we haven’t built those things. We haven’t provided housing you could afford. We haven’t provided abundant clean energy at the level we need.
Prop 45 is on the ballot because a state that can’t build what it promises isn’t protecting the environment. It’s not creating cleaner water. It’s protecting the status quo. And that’s really what Prop 45 was about. It’s about shaking up that status quo.
We have the toughest environmental rules in America, in California. I worked in government for 18 years. I helped craft a number of those environmental rules. I’m very proud of those.
Proposition 45 leaves every single environmental protection that’s in law today — leaves it intact. That’s true for laws that protect against paving over prime agricultural land. It’s true about laws that protect against paving over wetlands. It’s true about laws that protect against clear-cutting in our forests. All of those laws continue to exist untouched by Proposition 45.
What Proposition 45 does do is it ends the acceptance of endless delay as the status quo. As I said, I’ve worked in California politics and state and local government for 17, 18 years before I left and founded my firm. No one ever once said to me, California builds things way too fast. That’s never been the problem, right?
Our inability to execute against our own environmental and housing goals erodes our credibility to lead on environmentalism and inclusion. Prop 45 speeds up schools. It speeds up electricity projects and water without sacrificing any environmental review.
I just want to make one sort of clarification. This is less an argument about Prop 45 and more just a thing that I think would maybe be helpful for the listeners.
CEQA, as Ethan described it, he described what CEQA is, I think, very well. CEQA is environmental review. What CEQA is not is land-use decision-making or environmental regulation setting.
So in California, the state government and local governments decide where they wanna put housing, and then they zone for it. They decide how much new electricity infrastructure and where they want schools, and they zone for those things. The state has planning processes around providing clean water to people. They decide how to deploy money.
All of those processes, all of the land-use processes and the law-setting processes, are different than CEQA. Those happen through public process with public comment, publicly noticed meetings, and so forth, and years of council hearings. That’s a totally different thing than CEQA.
CEQA is the environmental review that occurs after a community has decided, we think this is where housing should go. We wanna get water infrastructure, we wanna get a new hospital built here.
Once the community has decided we’re gonna zone this parcel of land over here for a hospital, developers do their thing or public agencies do their thing and bring a project forward. And then CEQA is the safety review at the end of that planning process.
So I think it’s really important for people to understand that Proposition 45 doesn’t touch, or purport to touch in any way, the land-use planning powers that state and local governments have. They — every data center was mentioned in the intro. Proposition 45 does not cover data centers, period. We can have a longer conversation about that.
Laura Klivans: Yeah, we’ll talk about that in a little bit.
Jason Elliott: But just to make the point, and I won’t fight that fight right now because I’m sure it’ll come up. If a community doesn’t want a data center in their city, just don’t zone for one, just don’t approve one. And then CEQA is irrelevant because the underlying land use won’t allow for that data center.
And I think that’s a key point to make, is that we’re gonna keep differentiating because opponents of this measure obscure that line to try to be hyperbolic. I think it’s important to pull those things apart.
Land-use authority, what goes in your community, remains the power of your mayor, your city council, your board of supervisors. Prop 45 doesn’t impact that.
Laura Klivans: We’re hearing from Jason Elliott. He’s the president of policy consulting firm Versus Solutions. We also have Jordan Grimes here, the legislative director with environmental nonprofit Greenbelt Alliance.
Jordan, what we’ve just heard is largely an argument around streamlining CEQA. It is not about the decision around land use, as Jason’s telling us. What about Prop 45 concerns you? You’re part of the Know on Prop 45 campaign.
Jordan Grimes: Yes, thank you so much for having me back. Great to be here.
You know, there are many, I would say, problematic aspects with the measure. It’s hard to know where to start with, I think, the things that are most concerning.
You know, to step back, as we are discussing both with Jason and with Ethan, the Environmental Quality Act is fundamentally this law that provides protection to communities. It’s not about delay, although certainly that has been a tactic that bad actors have used. But fundamentally, it is about review. It is about looking at and analyzing whether or not there’s potential for environmental harm and then requiring mitigation of that harm.
And so it is the first line of defense for many communities. And ultimately, what Prop 45 does is strip away many of the protections inherent in that law.
The timelines, I think, are some of the most reasonable pieces of the initiative, although, again, it doesn’t differentiate between size of projects. It doesn’t differentiate, I think, between geography, where a project is, if it’s in a greenfield, if you’re paving over open space, or if you are in a city, for example. So I think that is inherently problematic in the initiative.
Laura Klivans: Will Jordan tell us what those timelines are?
Jordan Grimes: Yeah, the explicit timelines in the initiative are, generally speaking, 365 days for a full environmental impact report. Okay. You know, there are other timelines dependent on the type of environmental review, some jargony acronyms that we won’t get into too much, as we sort of discussed.
Jason Elliott: Basically —
Laura Klivans: Jargon for this.
It’s basically putting a time limit on the environmental review and then also curtailing lawsuits around it, right? But it’s not just letting them go on for an indefinite period of time.
Jordan Grimes: Exactly. And we’ve talked about that, but it’s actually quite a bit more than that.
Laura Klivans: What are the other concerns you have with it?
Jordan Grimes: Quite a few. I think the most concerning one for me is a new private right of action for developers to be able to sue municipalities if they deny a project or if they require sort of different mitigations that the developer views as unlawful.
That’s something that is a huge change to CEQA, that is to the Environmental Quality Act, that isn’t there right now. There’s also a provision that basically says if there is a conflict between other environmental laws, that the initiative provisions prevail.
There are provisions that severely limit what a court can consider and that severely limits what a court can consider even after — even if environmental harm has been found. The court is very limited in its remedies under the initiative.
So there are, I think, a litany of different things with this measure that go far beyond the timelines, many of which I think would be reasonable for certain projects. If we are talking about an apartment building in San Francisco, for example, the timelines that the initiative have in place might even be too long. It might not even make sense to do a year for an apartment project in Hayes Valley.
Laura Klivans: Okay.
Jordan Grimes: Um, but if you’re talking about, uh, a new, you know, exurban development in the wildland-urban interface in a high-fire area, um, one of your, uh, I would say probably wouldn’t be enough.
Laura Klivans: I want to go to a caller now. We have Jim in Richmond. Jim, welcome to Forum . Thanks for calling in.
Jim: Yeah, thank you, and thank you for holding the show. As somebody who has read CEQA documents here in the Bay Area on really, frankly, bad projects, I want to tell you that as a citizen, we will — and even the city will — approach a developer to try to cause less damage to habitat or traffic, and without CEQA, or without the ability to challenge it, this really feels like one of those TV shows where you’re running across a lake and you’re competing against people, you know, jumping across these rubber balls or whatever.
It’s so many obstacles. It just seems impossible at this point. It really feels undemocratic. And I’d like you to address the cost of this as reported in the state pamphlet. Thank you.
Laura Klivans: Thank you. Jason, can you address this? Does it take away someone’s ability to challenge?
Jason Elliott: And thanks for the call, Jim. I appreciate your advocacy.
No, it doesn’t take away someone’s ability to challenge it. Let me draw an analogy. I mean, I could go through the provision measure by measure, but this show isn’t long enough. So let me draw an analogy.
If you think about CEQA and the environmental impact report, so CEQA requires big projects to do the environmental impact report, which is what Ethan had laid out at the top of the hour. Think about the environmental impact report like the SAT test that we probably all endured when we were high schoolers.
The question — Prop 45 doesn’t make the questions on the SAT easier. It doesn’t allow you to skip the SAT and go straight to college. Proposition 45 doesn’t limit any of those things.
What Proposition 45 does is say, once you’ve done the SAT, the grader — the state, the city — has a timeline in which they have to grade the SAT and give you your score back, so you can go ahead and apply to college in a timely fashion.
It’s a timeline, right? It also says that while the grader’s grading your SAT test, the grader can’t say, well, you know, we don’t think that that’s how calculus works anymore. We’re gonna just, like, change one of the rules about log functions. And so you kind of have — you have to start over on the SAT.
That’s how CEQA works today. The way CEQA works is you can finish your environmental impact report with mitigations to make sure that you’re having that conversation with community and local government, get rid of the worst parts of a project that are the most harmful to communities, right?
All of that stays intact. All of the mitigation processes, all of that public feedback all stays intact. But once you’re done with that EIR, with that SAT test, it gets graded in a timely fashion, so you can build your project.
In our case, we estimate that it will cut the time for projects with EIRs in half, from about 3.1 years to about one and a half years. So it’s half the time, but all the protections.
And I think that’s the key point: it doesn’t strip away any protections. It doesn’t eliminate CEQA. So what I heard in Jim’s question was, Prop 45 would eliminate the public’s ability to raise these concerns. It won’t eliminate it. That’s a misconception, so I want to address that.
But it does say that let’s get this stuff done in a timely fashion, so that we can get good projects approved.
And last point I’ll make on this, Proposition 45 leaves intact every local government’s ability to reject an EIR and reject the project. There are no automatic approvals anywhere in Proposition 45. So if a developer brings forward a truly bad environmental project, the city council could just go ahead and reject it and reject the EIR and/or reject the underlying project.
Laura Klivans: Jordan, how does this sound for you when we’re thinking about what Jim is saying, the ability to challenge a project? Do you feel like it would be harder when Prop 45, if it passes?
Jordan Grimes: Absolutely. A hundred percent. You’re significantly limiting in terms of what the public is allowed to comment on, right? There are provisions that severely limit public comment. You are limiting the timelines in which the public comments are made.
Laura Klivans: Do it for —
Jason Elliott: It’s a time limitation. It’s not a qualitative limitation, so let’s make sure we’re accurate about what the measure does.
Laura Klivans: Right, but it does put a date —
Jason Elliott: Like the amount of days, okay?
Laura Klivans: Yes, it’s a time limit, not a subjective limit.
Jordan Grimes: You are limited in terms of vesting. If environmental conditions change on the ground, you are locked into a certain vesting schedule. So basically, things would go — everything would shift.
So, for example, right now, if an EIR was being conducted and conditions changed —
Laura Klivans: That’s the environmental impact report.
Jordan Grimes: Yes. Sorry about the jargon. If an environmental impact report was being conducted and conditions on the ground shifted in terms of habitat, in terms of various other things, right now, as the process works, those things can be considered.
The way the initiative would change the Environmental Quality Act would mean that you could not consider those. The conditions on the ground at the time of the project application would be locked in.
Laura Klivans: Like, read the very start.
Jordan Grimes: Exactly. And then the last thing I’ll just say is, yes, a city council or local jurisdiction could deny a project, with the potential that a developer could sue. And so there’s this chilling effect now under this new private right of action, right, where a municipality would have to weigh, do we want to deny this project? Do we want to risk getting sued by a project developer?
And again, we’re not just talking about projects that are potentially environmentally beneficial, right? You know, new housing in places we want to see it, bike lanes, public transit. We’re talking about some really potentially harmful projects.
Jason Elliott: Schools, clinics, hospitals, parks.
Jordan Grimes: Clean energy, clean water facilities.
Laura Klivans: Sure, that’s the side that’s a —
But I’ve also seen the no side saying, well, what about freeway expansion? We’re talking, like, we’re talking —
Jordan Grimes: Is that also included? Freeway expansions are absolutely included. We’re talking about CO2 pipelines. We are talking about exurban developments in high-fire areas. There’s a lot of different things that this project allows. Some of them are good. Some of them, I think, deserve that streamlining.
What we are looking at is, on net, is this better than the status quo? And our calculation is absolutely not.
Laura Klivans: Okay, okay. We’re gonna go to — we’re going to go to a caller, and then there’s lots of time to talk about these different things.
Okay. Lisa, we are going to go to you in San Francisco. Lisa, thank you for calling.
Lisa: Good morning. My head is spinning.
Laura Klivans: You’re not the only one.
Lisa: Yeah. This is a great debate, but I think for me, in this horrific time where, you know, these astroturf super PACs pop up named, you know, Neighborhoods for San Francisco or whatever. And it’s the real estate lobby or the apartment owners association or what have you, or developers, market-rate developers.
What I want to know from both of your guests, the proponent and the opponent, I would like to know who the major sponsors pro and their money, and I would like to know who are the sponsors against? Because we know that organizations like the San Francisco — the Sierra Club has been captured by real estate forces. I mean, everything is through the looking glass now.
So who are the funders of this initiative?
Laura Klivans: That’s a great question. Streamline, I’m triggered. Yes, there’s millions of dollars behind this initiative.
So actually, I know you were asking to go to Jason and Jordan. I’m gonna actually see if Ethan, if you could answer this one. Ethan Elkind with UC Berkeley, where’s the money coming from from both sides?
Ethan Elkind: Yeah, I don’t have encyclopedic knowledge, but I have looked at the backers. I mean, you have the Building Industry Association as a major backer of this. They’re the big sprawl developers in the state. You have the Chamber of Commerce supporting this initiative.
You basically have a lot of industry groups that are supporting this. On the con side, you’ve got environmental groups, and then you’ve got labor unions that often use CEQA as leverage to try to get project labor agreements, uh… for their union members, uh… And then, you know, it’s a grab bag of other folks, but I’m sure Jordan and Jason could speak in more detail. But that’s the general gist on the yes and the no side.
Laura Klivans: We’re going to come back to that because we’re about to take a break. This is Forum . I’m Laura Klivans in for Mina Kim. We’re talking about Proposition 45, a ballot measure proposing changes to California’s landmark environmental protection law.
And we’re joined by Ethan Elkind of UC Berkeley, Jason Elliott, president of the policy consulting firm Versus Solutions, and Jordan Grimes, legislative director with environmental nonprofit Greenbelt Alliance.
And we want to hear from you. How are you planning to vote on Prop 45 and why? I want to go to a question that comes from listener Jeff. Jeff writes, “To what extent do the guests believe the passage of Prop 45 will meaningfully change the speed of development, and in what sectors? Is that clean energy, roads, housing?”
Jason, let’s go to you.
Jason Elliott: Sure. Well, we do believe that it will speed up development, and that’s the purpose for crafting this measure. And speeding up development, let me say why that’s important.
Speed on its own is not necessarily a good thing. But when you have housing and clean energy and clean water projects, hospital projects, school projects that are delivered faster, that creates cost savings for local governments.
Of the non-housing projects that this measure covers, 76% of them that we expect would be covered by EIRs are projects that are brought forward by your local government, by your city, by your county. Fiscal Impact Methodology for Residential Construction
Estimates of the state and local tax revenues generated during the residential construction period were developed based on the publicly available economic data, state and local tax rates in effect as of FY 2024 – 2025, and IMPLAN model data on the number of wage and salary jobs supported by a given level of development activity (excluding any “multiplier” economic impacts).
Personal Income Tax
Construction period development activity generates PIT revenue from three payer types: employees paid wages or salary by construction firms; the proprietors of these firms; and the partners of impacted S-Corps, who pay PIT on their corporation’s pass-through income.
PIT from Employees
Estimated PIT revenue from wage and salary employees was derived from IMPLAN’s reported estimates of the number of wage and salary jobs supported by direct construction activity. IMPLAN’s aggregation of data collected by the federal Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) shows the distribution of occupation types (e.g., executives, administrative assistants, construction laborers) for each industry (e.g., construction, professional services, manufacturing) in California along with the average annual compensation paid to that occupation in each industry. PIT revenues for workers in each occupation were based on FTB data showing the average effective PIT rate imposed on PIT payers across various Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) buckets over the 2014 – 2020 period (e.g., Californians earning $60,000 – $80,000 faced a 2.7% average rate). 57
PIT from Proprietor Employment
IMPLAN also estimates the share of total construction sector expenditures that is earned as income by proprietors of construction firms. The estimated effective PIT rate paid on this income was based on annual business income data from the FTB. 58 Specifically, the weighted average effective tax rate for business income was calculated across all AGI buckets from 2014 through 2020, with weights applied to the rate for each AGI bucket based on the total amount of net business income for that AGI bucket. This methodology resulted in an overall effective tax rate of 4.26% on net business income.
Pass-Through Income from S-Corps
Estimation of the PIT revenue associated with S-Corps’ pass-through income was based on the same detailed annual FTB data described above. The weighted average effective PIT rate paid on pass-through income and partnership profits was 9.32% for the period from 2014 through 2020. This rate was applied to 98.5% of the estimated S-Corp share of corporate profits reported by IMPLAN (i.e., total S-Corp profits less the 1.5% paid as corporate income tax).
Corporation Tax
Estimates of corporation tax revenues were based on IMPLAN estimates of the corporate profits generated by construction firms. Total corporate profits were allocated to S-Corps and C-Corps in proportion to the share of total construction sector business receipts collected by each corporation type as of 2015, based on data published by the IRS’s Statistics of Income (SOI) program.
The state corporate income tax revenues generated by these profits is based on data published by the State of California Franchise Tax Board (FTB). S-Corps pay a 1.5% rate on in-state profits (with the remaining 98.5% treated as pass-through income subject to the personal income tax), while an analysis of FTB data shows that C-Corps paid an average effective corporate income tax rate of 2.4% on their in-state profits over the 2013 – 2022 period (lower than the 8.84% statutory rate due to various deductions and tax credits and the ability to carry over net losses from prior years). 59
Sales Tax: State General Fund and Local Shares
Sales tax revenue estimates were derived by multiplying the applicable sales tax rate by the estimated total taxable sales generated by the estimated annual development cost. The increase in taxable sales attributable to this total estimated development cost was based on the total value of intermediate inputs purchased by construction firms from their suppliers, as estimated by IMPLAN. For non-taxable inputs (e.g., services), the estimated purchase amount was excluded from the sales tax base estimate.
State General Fund sales tax revenues were calculated by multiplying the estimated increase in taxable sales by the General Fund’s base sales tax rate (i.e., 3.9375%). Local sales tax revenues are based on a combined local rate of 4.97%, which includes the Bradley-Burns rate (1.25%), the Public Safety Fund rate (0.50%), and the 1991 and 2011 Realignment shares (1.5625% combined), and the weighted average district tax rate across all local governments in California (1.66%). 60
EIR Cost Sample
The Non-Residential EIR Cost Sample includes all non-residential EIR projects in essential project categories that circulated a draft EIR between January 1, 2025, and December 31, 2025. Across all project construction types (i.e., including non-essential categories and residential construction), 281 EIRs were circulated during this period. Residential projects as well as non-essential non-residential projects (223 projects total) were then removed from the sample based on review of each EIR project’s “development type” data field on CEQANet. Of the remaining 58 projects in essential project categories, 10 projects relating to master plan updates or programmatic EIRs (PEIRs) were removed from the sample (since these project types do not involve specific development proposals for which costs can be estimated). As a result, the final analysis sample included 48 essential projects.
For each of the projects in the Cost Sample, total development costs were determined based on public project filing data, news reports or descriptions of the development (e.g., square footage, megawatts of solar capacity installed) and typical per-unit construction costs (e.g., dollars per square foot, dollars per megawatt) published in public surveys or other studies. To ensure that the expected costs of proposed megaprojects would not result in overestimates of the EIR project share of total non-residential project spending, the reported costs for these projects were reduced by 75%. 61
Summary of Prop 45’s Non-Timeline Procedural Reforms
In addition to establishing enforceable timelines, Prop 45 introduces other reforms intended to reduce delays associated with the preparation of EIRs and associated litigation that could further reduce review period timelines and reduce review costs for local governments. These reforms target well-documented sources of review-related costs imposed on project developers.
Streamlined Alternatives Analysis
Prop 45 would allow EIR project sponsors to elect to use a streamlined “alternatives analysis” during CEQA review, which would limit the range of alternative projects analyzed in an EIR. 62 By constraining the number of different projects analyzed, this option may reduce the costs of generating alternative designs, conducting technical studies, drafting the EIR, and responding to public comments.
Exclusion of late comments
Prop 45 would require that public comments be filed at least 72 hours prior to a proposed project’s public hearing related to its CEQA approval; late-submitted comments would be excluded from the administrative record. 63 Currently, project opponents may submit comments to lead agencies following the conclusion of the formal public review period, in some cases just hours prior to a public hearing on the project’s approval. These late comments impose added costs on lead agencies and project sponsors by requiring additional analyses and responses and may delay hearings to afford the lead agency sufficient time to respond. 64
Limits on the scope of legal challenges
Prop 45 would limit any CEQA-related litigation to allegations that a project’s approval conflicted with “objective, quantifiable, and written standards” that were in effect when the project’s application was submitted. This provision would reduce the number of CEQA-related legal challenges brought against projects sponsored by local agencies and could further reduce the expense of CEQA review itself. 65

Given the long tail of CEQA review periods above the project mean (as shown for the status quo EIR review periods in Figure 6), the distributions of non-EIR status quo review period durations were modeled as right-skewed lognormal distributions, in which most projects cluster near the median while a small share take substantially longer. (The modeled lognormal fit was validated against the EIR project sample, where the observed standard deviation of log review durations (0.847) closely matches the value implied by fitting a lognormal distribution to the sample mean and standard deviation (0.838).) For each non-EIR project type, the distribution’s mean was set equal to the AEP-reported mean review duration. The distribution’s standard deviation was estimated by applying the coefficient of variation for the EIR project sample under the status quo, i.e., the EIR sample’s standard deviation (1,151 days) divided by its mean (1,141 days), or approximately 1.01. As a result, for MND projects, the distribution’s status quo mean is eight months (or 240 days) and the standard deviation is 242 days (i.e., 1.01 × 240). Estimations of these reductions were calculated by simulating project samples for each non-EIR project type based on the mean and standard deviation parameters detailed above. As for EIR projects, post-Prop 45 average review durations and volatility measures for each non-EIR project type were calculated by applying Prop 45’s time limits to simulated projects with status quo review periods exceeding these limits.
As with EIR projects, it is conservatively assumed that Prop 45 would not affect the average duration of the non-EIR entitlement reviews outside the CEQA process.
See Note 12 for detail on the calculation of the volatility measure.

Estimation of each CEQA project type’s share of total permitting is based on AEP survey results (see the “Percent of Units” column in Figure 12). Though the AEP’s survey findings relate to the permitting of 5+ unit multifamily buildings, there is no publicly available data that reports CEQA project type permitting shares across all types of residential construction (i.e., including single-family homes and smaller multifamily buildings). AEP-based estimates of these shares may therefore overstate or understate a CEQA project type’s actual share. However, it is unlikely that a CEQA review type’s share of 5+ unit permitting differs substantially from its permitting share across all units. For example, given that many new single-family homes are developed as part of large subdivisions, it is likely that EIR projects also account for a significant share of single-family unit permits.

YIMBY Action Debated Prop 45. Here's Why We Couldn't Make Up Our Mind
Prop 45 has split the people who care about building more homes in California, including YIMBY Action's own leaders, who have not come to consensus on the measure that would limit the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA).
On September 30, we brought both sides together, moderated by Leora Tanjuatco Ross, the California Director of YIMBY Action.
Arguing Yes on Prop 45 were:
Emma Manoukian Chung, Director, BCFS
Kelsey Brewer, VP of Business Development, Jamboree Housing
Arguing No on Prop 45 were:
Jordan Grimes, Legislative Director, Greenbelt Alliance
Gabe Ross, Shute, Mihaly & Weinberger
Here's what they said, and what you wanted to know.
What Prop 45 Would do
Prop 45 would change how CEQA applies to "essential projects" like housing, roads, bridges, schools, broadband connections, wildfire prevention efforts, clean energy production, and more. It would set a 365-day deadline for environmental review, require courts to resolve related lawsuits within 270 days, and create a 90-day shot clock for any other permits a project would need. It does not exempt projects from CEQA, so review and mitigation would still be required.
The Yes Case: Certainty from Start to Finish
Manoukian Chung opened by framing Prop 45 as an affordability measure: "Every month that a project sits in the approval process, costs go up," she said, costs that land on all of us through higher rents, mortgages, and utility bills. She cited one estimate that permitting delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new California home.
A CEQA deadline, she stressed, "does not mean automatic approval." Cities and state agencies could still condition or deny projects. But the reforms could shave two to ten-plus years off approvals for essential projects, and allow the creation of at least 20,000 additional homes a year. "20,000 homes a year will not solve California's housing shortage," she said, "but it is meaningful progress year after year."
Manoukian Chung also asked YIMBYs to look hard at who is backing the No side, pointing to the building trades and the Sierra Club, groups she said have spent years "fighting tooth and nail" against housing and permitting reform.
Brewer brought the developer's view. "I think I'm the only actual affordable housing developer here on the call," she said. “There are many factors that AB 130 doesn't cover. The Swiss cheese approach to CEQA reform isn’t working.”
The No case: a fast lane for sprawl
Ross argued that Prop 45 "fundamentally isn't a reform measure." His problem was that it would lower the bar for everything at once: sprawl and infill, market-rate and affordable, freeways and mass transit. "What we need to be doing is improving processes for the kind of housing that we want," he said.
He also warned that because Prop 45 is an initiative, the State Legislature couldn’t amend it. Even small, technical material in it would be "stuck for a generation." His prediction: "Prop 45 is going to look like our generation's Prop 13 not very long from now."
Grimes, a lead with Peninsula for Everyone, went further. "I personally believe as a YIMBY that Prop 45 represents a major threat to our movement," he said. His argument: we just won SB 79 and AB 130, which exempted infill housing from CEQA, and more than 15,000 units have already been permitted under AB 130. Prop 45, he said, would "explode sprawl development in California."
Where We Clashed
Is AB 130 enough?
Throughout the debate, Grimes said AB 130 so many times he joked he'd "get it tattooed on my forehead." His case was that it was "the most sweeping reform the state of California has ever done," and the Legislature keeps adding exemptions to CEQA, from SB 423 and AB 2011 to this year's bills for student housing and hospitals.
In response, Brewer rejected the idea that AB 130 was enough to fast-track housing at the rate we need it: "It's simply not true, Jordan."
The Yes side continued to name three gaps in AB 130. Manoukian Chung said AB 130's infill exemption only covers sites under 20 acres, opponents can still sue over whether an exemption applies, and post-CEQA permitting takes nearly a year longer than CEQA review itself (438 days on average for multifamily housing in San Francisco, she said). She noted that Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, who drove AB 130, also supports Prop 45.
Data centers
The moderator went off script to ask both sides a yes-or-no question: Would Prop 45 apply to data centers? The Yes side said absolutely not. Data centers aren't one of the eight essential categories, and calling them "broadband" projects would make every building with Wi-Fi a broadband project. Grimes countered that legal scholars at UC Berkeley and UC Davis say there are situations where data centers would qualify. "This is clearly going to be litigated," he said.
Q&A Portion
Will Wright asked why the Legislature hasn't passed something as comprehensive as Prop 45 would be. The Yes side said organized labor blocks system-wide CEQA reform in Sacramento, which is why we get piecemeal bills. Grimes said nothing as "sweeping" as Prop 45 has been tried, but pointed to targeted wins like AB 205's shot clock for clean energy. [Fact check: AB 130 was as sweeping as Prop 45, and it never would’ve passed the Legislature without Governor Newsom putting his finger on the scale.]
Chris Tokita asked what CEQA actually does for the environment. Ross said its real teeth is mitigation: It's the hook cities use to require fixes for a project's harms, and Prop 45 would leave them "with no way to provide that protection." Brewer called that "a NIMBY argument," because cities could still impose conditions of approval under Prop 45. Manoukian Chung added that CEQA currently slows down wildfire prevention and clean energy projects, which Prop 45 would speed up.
Meanwhile, in the chat
The chat was its own debate, with more than 200 messages. Some highlights:
Attendees went straight to the text on data centers. One of them pasted the proposition’s definition of an "essential broadband internet access project." Another argued its language about transmitting data to "all or substantially all internet endpoints" clearly meant internet service providers. Others asked where a judge would draw the line. Both sides posted legal analysis:Prop 45 does not cover data centers (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/08/19/https-www-dailyjournal-com-article-393806-california-s-proposition-45-does-not-cover-data-centers/) (via the Yes campaign),Prop 45 will speed data center construction (https://www.dailyjournal.com/articles/394431-prop-45-will-speed-data-center-construction), andBerkeley Law professor Eric Biber's take (https://legal-planet.org/2026/09/10/more-on-baca-and-data-centers/).
Can the Legislature fix it later? Several people noted lawmakers can amend an initiative with a two-thirds vote, as long as the changes are consistent with its intent. Whether that's "hard" or "virtually impossible" was, of course, debated.
Fix CEQA or go for the kill? One attendee summed it up: The No side wants to fix CEQA, the Yes side wants "to go for the kill." Replies split, from "Prop 45 is what fixes CEQA" to "You can hate CEQA and vote 'no' on Prop 45."
What's the real divide? One attendee put it this way: "For those of us who believe all housing is good housing, Prop 45 is an easy yes. For those who believe that only 'quality' housing should be built, Prop 45 is a hard no." Others pushed back that Prop 45 covers energy and highway projects too, so it's about much more than housing.
Sprawl got its own thread. Some argued sprawl doesn't pay for itself (one shared California YIMBY's post on howsprawl costs the U.S. $1 trillion a year (https://cayimby.org/blog/sprawl-costs-the-u-s-1-trillion-every-year/)). An ecological restoration professional countered that much of the land in question is already-degraded farmland, not "pristine redwood forests."
Closing Arguments, and Where we Landed
The closers both started with common ground. "All of us care about the same thing," Brewer said, "which is building enough housing for the people that live here and for future generations." Grimes closed for the other side with his own story. He grew up in the Bay Area, watched too little housing get built, and saw himself getting priced out. He's opposing Prop 45, he said, because sprawl will be its main housing beneficiary. He noted that California YIMBY, Streets For All, and East Bay for Everyone have either opposed the measure or stayed neutral. "We have to choose infill or sprawl," he said, "and I urge folks to choose infill."
Right after the debate, YIMBY Action’s volunteer chapter Leads voted on a recommendation. It takes 60% of leads agreeing for our organization to take a position, and they did not reach consensus. So YIMBY Action is not endorsing either side of Prop 45.
This is what a big-tent movement looks like. Smart, committed YIMBYs looked at the same measure and came out in different places. Make your own call on November 3. And if you want a voice in decisions like this one,become a YIMBY Action member (https://yimbyaction.org/?form=ceqa-debate).
